questions.text: The 'master gland' of the endocrine system, which controls most other endocrine glands, is the ____.

options.text: Pituitary gland — located at the base of the brain
Thyroid gland — located in the front of the neck
Adrenal gland — located above each kidney
Pineal gland — located deep within the brain

questions.explanation: The pituitary gland (hypophysis), attached to the hypothalamus at the brain's base, is called the 'master gland' because its hormones (TSH, FSH, LH, ACTH, GH, ADH) regulate most other endocrine glands. The hypothalamus itself regulates the pituitary, making it the true 'master of the master.'

questions.text: Insulin is secreted by the pancreas when blood glucose levels rise. What is insulin's primary function?

options.text: Stimulates cells to absorb glucose, lowering blood sugar levels
Stimulates the liver to release stored glucose into the bloodstream
Stimulates glucagon release to increase metabolic activity
Stimulates the adrenal glands to prepare the body for stress

questions.explanation: Insulin (secreted by β-cells of pancreatic islets of Langerhans) stimulates cells to take up glucose and promotes glycogen synthesis in liver and muscles — lowering blood glucose. Glucagon (from α-cells) does the opposite: raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogenolysis. Type 1 diabetes = insufficient insulin production.

questions.text: Iodine deficiency causes goitre — an enlargement of the thyroid gland. Why does the thyroid gland enlarge when iodine is deficient?

options.text: The gland enlarges as a compensatory attempt to trap more iodine for hormone synthesis
Excess iodine builds up inside the gland, causing it to swell physically
Pituitary TSH levels fall, causing the thyroid to atrophy and appear enlarged
Iodine deficiency directly triggers inflammatory thyroiditis causing swelling

questions.explanation: Thyroid hormones (T3, T4) require iodine. When iodine is deficient, T3/T4 production falls → the pituitary releases more TSH (feedback loop) → TSH stimulates the thyroid to grow, enlarging it in a compensatory attempt to capture more iodine. This negative feedback-driven enlargement is goitre. Prevention: iodised salt.

questions.text: Adrenaline (epinephrine), released by the adrenal medulla, is known as the 'fight-or-flight' hormone. Which of the following is NOT an effect of adrenaline?

options.text: Increased heart rate and blood pressure for action readiness
Dilation of pupils to improve visual awareness in threat
Slowing of digestion to redirect blood to muscles during stress
Stimulating insulin release to lower blood glucose for calm recovery

questions.explanation: Adrenaline does the opposite of option D: it RAISES blood glucose (by stimulating glycogenolysis) to fuel muscles during fight-or-flight. It does NOT stimulate insulin release — that would lower blood glucose, the opposite of what is needed in an emergency. Options A, B, C are all genuine fight-or-flight responses.

questions.text: Growth Hormone (GH), secreted by the anterior pituitary, stimulates bone and muscle growth. Excess GH in adults (after growth plates fuse) causes ____.

options.text: Acromegaly — enlargement of hands, feet, and facial features
Gigantism — abnormally tall stature from birth onward
Dwarfism — stunted growth from insufficient bone elongation
Cushing's syndrome — central obesity from cortisol excess

questions.explanation: GH excess in ADULTS (fused growth plates) → acromegaly: coarsening of facial features, enlarged hands/feet/jaw. GH excess in CHILDREN (open growth plates) → gigantism (abnormal height). Dwarfism = GH deficiency in childhood. Cushing's = cortisol excess (from adrenal or pituitary ACTH excess), not GH.

questions.text: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) and calcitonin have opposing effects on blood calcium levels. Which correctly describes their actions?

options.text: PTH raises blood calcium (from bones/kidneys); calcitonin lowers it (promotes bone storage)
PTH lowers blood calcium by promoting kidney excretion; calcitonin raises it
Both PTH and calcitonin raise blood calcium through different mechanisms
PTH is released when calcium is high; calcitonin is released when calcium is low

questions.explanation: PTH (from parathyroid glands): released when blood Ca²⁺ is LOW → mobilises Ca from bones, increases kidney reabsorption of Ca, activates vitamin D → RAISES blood Ca. Calcitonin (from thyroid C-cells): released when blood Ca²⁺ is HIGH → promotes calcium deposition in bones → LOWERS blood Ca. They form a calcium homeostasis antagonistic pair.

questions.text: The hypothalamus-pituitary axis controls hormone release via negative feedback. In this system, ____.

options.text: rising hormone levels suppress hypothalamic/pituitary output, preventing overproduction
rising hormone levels stimulate more hypothalamic output in a positive feedback loop
the pituitary acts independently; the hypothalamus only provides structural support
negative feedback only applies to sex hormones, not to thyroid or adrenal axes

questions.explanation: Negative feedback: when target gland hormone (e.g., cortisol, T3/T4, sex steroids) rises, it inhibits both the hypothalamic releasing hormone and pituitary tropic hormone → preventing overproduction. Example: high cortisol suppresses CRH (hypothalamus) and ACTH (pituitary). Positive feedback is rare (exception: LH surge during ovulation). This principle governs all three main endocrine axes (HPA, HPT, HPG).
